title: Why ChatGPT Keeps Interrupting You — Dr. Tom Shapland, LiveKit

summary: Tom Shapland, Product Manager at LiveKit, addresses Voice AI's interruption problem, calling it the biggest challenge facing voice AI agents. When ChatGPT Advanced Voice Mode interrupts users it's annoying, but when a voice AI dental assistant interrupts, the patient hangs up and the dentist stops paying—making it an industry-wide problem. Turn-taking—the unspoken system for controlling the conversational floor—is fundamentally hard because it happens very fast, varies across cultures (Danes take longer; Japanese respond almost instantaneously), across individuals, and within individuals based on emotional state. Current voice AI pipelines use cascading systems: audio chunks to speech-to-text, VAD determines if user finished speaking, transcript goes to LLM, then text-to-speech back to the user. VAD has two parts: a neural network detecting speech vs. not-speech, and a silence algorithm triggering end-of-turn after a threshold (e.g., half a second). Drawing on linguistics research, Shapland highlights that humans respond in ~200ms but speech generation takes ~600ms, implying predictive turn-end detection across three stages: semantic prediction, refinement, and prosody-based finalization. The human mind is full duplex—simultaneously processing input and generating output. New approaches augment VAD with models examining semantics, syntax, prosody, or acoustic features. LiveKit's semantic end-of-utterance model uses last 4 turns as input to a transformer predicting end-of-utterance tokens. Other approaches combine audio tokens and acoustic features: Daily's open-weight smart turn model, AssemblyAI's streaming STT with end-of-utterance likelihood, and QAI's similar model. A limitation of STT-built-in EOU models is they only see user speech, not agent speech—half the context. Even speech-to-speech models like OpenAI's real-time API still use VAD internally. ChatGPT interrupts because it thinks you're done based on silence duration or previous context. Full duplex models (Moshi, Meta's Sync LLM) are more like the human mind—always listening and generating, emitting natural silence when not speaking, and in Sync LLM's case forecasting ~5 tokens / 200ms ahead. However, they're small, poorly trained models that can't do instruction following well. Shapland predicts full duplex models won't solve production problems; instead, smarter VAD augmentations and faster cascade pipeline models will prevail. In Q&A, Shapland notes visual cues are low in the predictor stack—semantics is primary; TTS is the most expensive pipeline component; LiveKit's EOU model is open-weight and free; and the industry lacks a good turn-taking benchmark. He also addresses back channeling: LiveKit's current approach is simple—if a person speaks for more than X milliseconds, assume it's an interruption rather than a back channel. He wants to build an ML model to distinguish back channels from actual interruptions. Notably, Meta's Sync LLM can natively back channel (mhm, uhhuh) because it learned from raw audio data, which is a neat capability of full duplex models.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & the Interruption Problem
sections.summary: Shapland introduces Voice AI's interruption problem as the biggest challenge in voice AI agents. Interruptions in consumer products like ChatGPT are annoying, but in business contexts (e.g., dental assistants), they cause users to hang up and developers lose paying customers.

sections.title: Defining Turn-Taking & Its Difficulty
sections.summary: Turn-taking is defined as the unspoken system for controlling the conversational floor. It's hard because it happens fast, varies across cultures (Danes slower, Japanese almost instantaneous), across individuals, and within individuals based on emotional state.

sections.title: Current Voice AI Pipeline Overview
sections.summary: Shapland provides a simplified overview of the current voice AI pipeline: speech-to-text → VAD (determines if user finished) → LLM (chat completion) → text-to-speech → audio back to user.

sections.title: Voice Activity Detection (VAD) Details
sections.summary: VAD has two parts: a neural network detecting speech vs. not-speech, and a silence algorithm that triggers end-of-turn after a threshold (e.g., half a second). Most production systems use this approach, but new methods are emerging.

sections.title: Linguistics Research on Human Turn-Taking
sections.summary: Shapland explains the psycholinguistic puzzle: humans respond in ~200ms but speech generation takes ~600ms, implying prediction. Primary inputs are semantics, syntax, prosody, and visual cues. The exact mechanism is not fully understood.

sections.title: Three Stages of Human Turn-Taking
sections.summary: The accepted model of human turn-taking has three stages: semantic prediction (inferring intended message and predicting end-of-utterance), refinement (narrowing endpoint using semantics and syntax), and finalization (using prosody and acoustic features near turn end).

sections.title: Full Duplex Processing in the Human Mind
sections.summary: The human mind is full duplex—simultaneously comprehending input and generating output. A figure shows comprehension and production tracks running in parallel before the speaker's turn ends.

sections.title: Contrasting Human vs. AI, Cascading Models & LiveKit Demo
sections.summary: Current voice AI is much simpler than human turn-taking: backward-looking, serial, no prediction. New approaches augment VAD with semantic/syntactic/prosodic models. LiveKit's semantic end-of-utterance model takes last 4 turns as input to a transformer predicting end-of-utterance tokens. Shane's demo shows dramatic improvement over traditional VAD.

sections.title: Acoustic & Combined VAD Augmentation Approaches
sections.summary: Beyond text-based semantic models, new approaches use audio tokens and acoustic features to infer end-of-turn. Daily's open-weight smart turn model combines transformer and acoustic analysis. AssemblyAI's new streaming STT emits both transcript and end-of-utterance likelihood in one model. QAI has a similar release. A limitation: STT-built-in EOU models only see user speech, not agent speech—half the context. All approaches work remarkably well and are easy to implement.

sections.title: Speech-to-Speech Models & Answering the Title Question
sections.summary: Despite claims that speech-to-speech models will solve turn-taking, OpenAI's real-time API still uses VAD internally (with optional 'semantic VAD'). ChatGPT interrupts because it thinks you're done based on silence duration or previous context. The problem remains unsolved; OpenAI doesn't use LiveKit's EOU model despite LiveKit powering the audio transport.

sections.title: Full Duplex Models: Moshi & Sync LLM
sections.summary: Full duplex models process input and generate output simultaneously, like the human mind. Moshi always listens and always generates output, emitting natural silence when not speaking. Meta's Sync LLM forecasts ~5 tokens / 200ms ahead. Downside: these are small, poorly trained models that can't do instruction following well—impractical for production.

sections.title: Predictions for the Future
sections.summary: Shapland predicts full duplex models won't solve the problem for production use cases. Instead, smarter VAD augmentations and faster cascade pipeline models will prevail, giving developers more budget and control. Computers don't do math like humans, and LLMs think differently—voice AI won't use the same mechanisms as the human mind.

sections.title: Q&A Session
sections.summary: Q&A covers: demo truncation (full version on LiveKit Twitter); visual cues are low in the predictor stack—semantics is primary; TTS is the most expensive pipeline component; LiveKit's EOU model is open-weight and free; benchmarking turn-taking is difficult and the industry lacks a good benchmark. The final question addresses back channeling: LiveKit's current approach is simple—if a person speaks for more than X milliseconds, assume it's an interruption rather than a back channel. Shapland wants to build an ML model to distinguish back channels from actual interruptions. He notes Meta's Sync LLM can natively back channel (mhm, uhhuh) because it learned from raw audio data. Back channeling remains a tough problem.
